Oil was struck at Burgan, in the desert south of Kuwait town, in February 1938. The field turned out to be the second largest in the world, after Ghawar in Saudi Arabia.

The Kuwait Oil Company, owned by Anglo-Persian (later BP) and America's Gulf Oil, had drilled there after the finds in Bahrain. The war delayed production, and exports began in 1946.

Oil money quickly replaced pearling and the dhow trade. Kuwait became a welfare state with free schools, hospitals and jobs for citizens, and it took in workers from across the Arab world and South Asia. In 1991 retreating Iraqi troops set hundreds of wells alight in the Kuwaiti oil fires.
